exercises.title: Bài 1 · Farming systems around the world
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Agriculture is the cultivation of plants and the raising of animals for food, fibre and other products. It is the main source of income for hundreds of millions of rural households, and it is the basis of food security. Farming systems differ widely, but two broad types are usually distinguished. In subsistence farming, a family grows crops mainly for its own consumption and sells only a small surplus. In commercial farming, production is organised for the market, and farmers use machinery, improved seed, fertiliser and irrigation to increase yield.

Most farms in Asia are smallholdings of less than two hectares. A typical smallholder may grow rice in a paddy field during the rainy season, vegetables in the dry season and keep a few pigs and chickens; this combination is known as mixed farming. It spreads risk, because a poor harvest in one activity can be compensated by another. Larger plantations, by contrast, specialise in a single cash crop such as rubber, coffee or tea.

Good farming depends on practices that protect the soil. Crop rotation and intercropping keep the land productive, while monoculture, repeated year after year, may increase pests and exhaust nutrients. Irrigation provides water in the dry season, and drainage removes excess water during heavy rain. Many smallholders also join a cooperative, which allows them to buy inputs more cheaply and to negotiate better prices. Agricultural extension services support them by teaching new techniques.

content.q: In subsistence farming, a family grows crops mainly for its own consumption.
content.why: Đoạn 1: tự cung tự cấp = trồng chủ yếu để gia đình tiêu dùng.

content.q: Most farms in Asia are very large plantations.
content.why: Đoạn 2: hầu hết là nông hộ nhỏ **dưới hai héc-ta**.

content.q: Mixed farming spreads risk.
content.why: Đoạn 2: vụ thất bát ở một hoạt động được bù bằng hoạt động khác.

content.q: Monoculture always improves the soil.
content.why: Đoạn 3: độc canh lặp lại có thể **tăng sâu bệnh và làm cạn dinh dưỡng**.

opts: Machinery, improved seed, fertiliser and irrigation

content.q: What is mixed farming?
content.why: Đoạn 2: trồng trọt kết hợp chăn nuôi.
opts: Growing crops and keeping animals on the same farm

content.why: Đoạn 3: mua vật tư rẻ hơn, thương lượng giá tốt hơn.

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: A smallholder family in the Mekong Delta
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
The Nguyen family farms 1.5 hectares in the Mekong Delta. In the past they grew only rice, harvesting three crops a year and applying large amounts of fertiliser to maintain yield. Costs were rising, however, and the third crop earned little profit because the soil was becoming less fertile and pests were more common.

Following advice from the local agricultural extension officer, the family changed its system. They now grow two rice crops a year, using certified seed and less fertiliser, and they use the third season for a rotation crop such as mung bean, which improves the soil. They have dug a small pond on part of the land, where they raise fish, and they keep ducks that feed on insects in the paddy field. Waste from the animals is used as manure. This mixed system gives them several sources of income during the year.

The family also joined a cooperative that buys rice from its members, dries it in a modern plant and sells it to an exporter. As a result, they receive a higher price than they used to receive from local traders. Mr Nguyen admits that the first year was difficult, because he had to learn new skills and borrow money for the pond. Nevertheless, farm income has increased by about 30 percent, and the family says that the land is healthier than before. The case shows how smallholders can improve both income and sustainability without increasing the size of their farms.

content.q: The family used to grow only rice.
content.why: Đoạn 1: trước đây họ chỉ trồng lúa.

content.q: They now grow three rice crops a year.
content.why: Đoạn 2: họ trồng **hai** vụ lúa, vụ thứ ba luân canh.

content.q: Waste from the animals is used as manure.
content.why: Đoạn 2: chất thải vật nuôi dùng làm phân chuồng.

content.q: Farm income has decreased.
Why did the third rice crop earn little profit?
content.why: Đoạn 1: đất kém màu mỡ hơn và sâu bệnh nhiều hơn.
opts: The soil was less fertile and pests were more common
There was too much rain only

content.q: What do they grow in the third season?
content.why: Đoạn 2: cây luân canh như đậu xanh.
opts: A rotation crop such as mung bean

content.q: What does the cooperative do?
content.why: Đoạn 3: mua lúa của thành viên, sấy và bán cho nhà xuất khẩu.
opts: Buys rice from members, dries it and sells it to an exporter

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Understanding soil fertility
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Soil is the foundation of crop production, and its fertility determines how well plants grow. A typical soil has several layers: the topsoil, which is darker and richer in organic matter, and the subsoil below it, which contains more minerals and less life. Soil texture depends on the proportion of sand, silt and clay. Sandy soil drains faster and warms up earlier than clay soil, but it holds fewer nutrients; clay soil retains more water and nutrients, but it can become waterlogged. Loam, a balanced mixture, is generally the best for most crops, while alluvial soil, which is deposited by rivers, is usually more fertile than upland soil.

Plants need large amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, which are supplied by NPK fertiliser, and smaller amounts of micronutrients such as zinc and boron. However, nutrients can be absorbed only within a suitable pH range; in strongly acidic soil, some are locked up and aluminium may harm roots. Farmers therefore test their soil and apply lime or organic matter where necessary. Compost, manure and green manure improve both fertility and structure, and they are often cheaper than chemical products over the long term.

Soil must also be protected. Erosion removes topsoil faster than nature can replace it, especially on steep slopes without vegetation, and compaction by heavy machinery reduces root growth. Mulching, terracing and no-till farming protect the surface, while crop rotation with legumes returns nitrogen to the soil. Efficient irrigation, such as drip irrigation, supplies water more precisely than flooding and increases water use efficiency.

content.q: Clay soil drains faster than sandy soil.

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: Restoring degraded land on a coffee hillside
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A group of coffee farmers in the Central Highlands noticed that yields on their steep hillsides were falling. Their soil, which had been cultivated for more than twenty years, was becoming thinner and more acidic. After every heavy rain, brown water ran down the slope, carrying away topsoil. A soil test carried out by the local extension service showed low organic matter, a pH of 4.2 and very little phosphorus.

With technical support, the farmers started a restoration programme. First, they built contour terraces and planted grass strips to slow the water. Lime was applied to raise the pH, and compost made from coffee husks and cattle manure was spread around each tree. Between the rows, they planted a green manure of legumes, which was cut regularly and used as mulch. Shade trees were also introduced, so the coffee plants were protected from extreme heat and the soil stayed moister. Drip irrigation replaced the old sprinklers, which had used much more water.

After three years, erosion had decreased sharply, and organic matter had risen from 1.5 to 3 percent. The soil was darker, looser and richer in earthworms. Yields were about 20 percent higher than before, and the beans were of better quality. The farmers also spent less on chemical fertiliser, although they had to invest more labour at the beginning. One farmer said that the most important lesson was that improving the soil is a long-term investment, not a quick fix.

content.why: Đoạn 1: năng suất trên sườn dốc đang giảm.

content.why: Đoạn 2: tưới nhỏ giọt thay thế hệ phun cũ.

content.q: The farmers spent more on chemical fertiliser.
content.why: Đoạn 3: họ chi **ít hơn** cho phân hóa học.

content.q: Why was brown water running down the slope?
content.why: Đoạn 1: mưa lớn cuốn trôi lớp đất mặt.
opts: Heavy rain was carrying away topsoil

content.q: What was lime used for?
content.why: Đoạn 2: bón vôi để nâng pH.

What was the farmer's main lesson?
content.why: Đoạn 3: cải tạo đất là khoản đầu tư dài hạn.
opts: Improving soil is a long-term investment

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Integrated pest management and post-harvest handling
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Pests and diseases cause large losses every year, but heavy use of chemicals is not the best solution. Insecticides kill natural enemies together with pests, and pests often develop resistance, so outbreaks may return in a more severe form. Residues on food can also harm consumers and make exports difficult. For these reasons, integrated pest management (IPM) has been promoted worldwide.

In IPM, the field is monitored regularly, and control measures are applied only when pest numbers exceed a threshold. Resistant varieties are planted, crops are rotated, and field hygiene is maintained. Natural enemies are protected, and in some cases they are released deliberately; pheromone traps are used to detect and catch insects such as fruit flies. When chemicals are necessary, a selective product is chosen, the correct dose is applied and the pre-harvest interval is respected. Protective equipment should always be worn by the sprayer.

Protection continues after harvest. In many developing countries, 10 to 30 percent of grain is lost between harvest and consumption because of poor drying, storage and handling. Grain must be dried quickly to a safe moisture content, otherwise moulds grow and produce mycotoxins. It is then stored in clean, dry silos or sealed bags, and protected from rats and insects. Fruit and vegetables are graded, packed carefully and kept in cold storage to slow ripening and extend their shelf life. Finally, traceability systems record where each lot was grown and treated, so that food safety problems can be identified quickly.

content.q: Insecticides can kill natural enemies together with pests.
content.why: Đoạn 1: thuốc trừ sâu giết cả thiên địch.

content.q: In IPM, chemicals are applied on a fixed calendar regardless of pest numbers.

exercises.passage:
A vegetable cooperative in the highlands supplied supermarkets, but in one season a shipment of cabbages was rejected because residues of an insecticide were found above the permitted level. The cooperative's investigation showed that several members had sprayed shortly before harvest, and that the pre-harvest interval had not been respected. The incident was a serious warning: if the problem was repeated, the cooperative would lose its contract.

With the help of an extension officer, the cooperative introduced IPM. Farmers were trained to scout their fields twice a week and to record pest counts on a card. Yellow sticky traps were placed at the field edges, and a biological product based on a bacterium was used against caterpillars. Chemicals were permitted only if the threshold was exceeded, and each application was entered in a logbook, which also recorded the date of harvest. Sprayers were provided with masks, gloves and boots, and empty containers were collected and disposed of safely.

Post-harvest handling was improved as well. The cabbages, which used to be piled on the ground in the sun, are now cut in the early morning, graded by size and packed in clean plastic crates. A small cold room was built, and the vegetables are cooled within two hours. Each crate carries a QR code that links to the farmer's record. Within a year, residue tests were all below the limit, pesticide costs fell by 25 percent and post-harvest losses dropped from 20 to 8 percent. Supermarkets increased their orders, and the cooperative received a higher price for its certified vegetables.

exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Disease is one of the greatest threats to livestock farming. A single outbreak of avian influenza or African swine fever can destroy a whole farm, and it may spread to neighbouring districts. Prevention is therefore much cheaper and more effective than treatment, and it depends on biosecurity: a set of measures that must be applied every day.

Basic biosecurity rules are simple. Visitors must not enter animal houses without permission, and those who do enter have to wear clean clothes and disinfect their footwear. Vehicles should be washed and disinfected at the gate. New animals must be kept in quarantine for at least two weeks, and sick animals have to be separated immediately. Wild birds, rodents and insects should be kept out, and dead animals must be removed and disposed of safely. Farmers do not have to build expensive facilities to begin with, but they must be consistent: one careless day can undo months of careful work.

Vaccination is another key tool, but it must follow the schedule recommended by a veterinarian. When antibiotics are used, the dose and the withdrawal period must be respected, because residues in meat, milk or eggs can harm consumers and encourage antimicrobial resistance. Good housing, clean water, balanced feed and low stocking density also reduce disease, and they improve animal welfare. Finally, farmers should keep records of births, treatments and movements, because authorities may ask for them during an outbreak.

A family in a northern province raises 8,000 broilers in two open-sided houses. One winter, an outbreak of avian influenza was confirmed on a farm three kilometres away. The local veterinary officer called the owner, Mr Tuan, and explained that he had to take immediate action: movement of birds and eggs must stop, all visitors must be banned and every vehicle had to be disinfected.

Mr Tuan followed the instructions strictly. He put a disinfectant footbath at the entrance of each house and provided overalls and boots that must not leave the farm. His workers had to change their clothes and wash their hands before entering the birds' area. Wild birds were kept out by nets, and rats were controlled around the feed store. When he noticed several birds with swollen heads and sudden deaths, he did not wait: he reported the symptoms to the veterinary officer, who took samples. The tests were negative, but the officer advised Mr Tuan to continue the measures for another three weeks.

The farm remained free of disease, and the flock was sold on time. Two months later, the owner invested in better fencing, a vehicle disinfection spray at the gate and a small quarantine house for new chicks. He also began to keep a daily record of mortality, feed intake and water consumption. 'In the past I thought biosecurity was a cost,' he said. 'Now I see it as insurance. Neighbours who ignored the rules lost everything.' The case shows that quick reporting, discipline and low-cost measures can protect a farm even when disease is nearby.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Why forests matter and how to manage them
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Forests cover about 30 percent of the world's land, and they provide far more than timber. They regulate water, because forest soil absorbs rain and releases it slowly into rivers; if a watershed is deforested, floods and landslides become more frequent. They store carbon, so they act as a carbon sink; if forests are cleared or burnt, this carbon returns to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. They are also home to most of the world's land-based biodiversity, from the canopy to the forest floor, and millions of people depend on non-timber forest products such as honey, bamboo and medicinal plants.

Forest management aims to obtain these benefits without destroying the resource. In sustainable forest management, the amount of wood harvested must not exceed the amount that grows back. Selective logging causes less damage than clear-cutting, and natural regeneration or planting from a nursery is used to replace harvested trees. In plantations, thinning and pruning improve the quality of timber, and the trees are harvested at the rotation age. Independent forest certification allows buyers to recognise wood from well-managed forests.

Threats are serious. Deforestation for agriculture, illegal logging and forest fires cause losses every year. If a firebreak is built and rangers patrol the area, fires can be detected and controlled more quickly. Local communities are often the best guardians: if they receive income from payment for forest ecosystem services or from agroforestry, they have a strong reason to protect the trees. Restoration through afforestation and reforestation can bring back some functions, but a new plantation will never be identical to a natural forest.

exercises.passage:
A coastal commune had lost most of its mangrove forest during the 1990s, when the trees were cleared for shrimp ponds. After a typhoon damaged the sea dyke and flooded several villages, the people realised that the mangroves had protected them. The commune decided to restore the forest, with help from a conservation project.

The first attempt, which used seedlings planted on the open mud, failed because the waves were too strong and many seedlings were washed away. Engineers then built low fences of bamboo to reduce wave energy, and villagers planted a mixture of species, because a diverse forest is more resilient than a single-species stand. A community forestry group was formed, and each family was responsible for one plot. If a family protected its plot and kept the survival rate above 80 percent, it received a small payment each year. The group also allowed controlled harvesting of crabs and honey, so that people could earn income without cutting trees.

After ten years, 300 hectares of mangrove had been restored. Fish, crabs and birds had returned, and the dyke needed less repair. In the next storm, the villages behind the forest suffered much less damage. However, the project leaders warn that the future is uncertain: if the community stopped managing the forest, shrimp farms might expand again, and if sea level rises quickly, young trees may not be able to adapt. They believe that the most important factor is that local people feel the forest belongs to them.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Aquaculture and capture fisheries
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Fish and other aquatic foods provide about 17 percent of the animal protein consumed worldwide, and they are especially important for people in developing countries. Two sectors supply this food. Capture fisheries catch wild fish, using vessels such as trawlers, purse seiners and small boats with gillnets or longlines, while aquaculture raises aquatic animals and plants in ponds, cages or tanks. Since the 1980s, catches from the sea have remained roughly stable, but aquaculture has grown rapidly, and today it produces about half of all fish for human consumption.

Many wild stocks have been overfished. When fishing pressure is too high, fish are caught faster than they can reproduce, and the stock declines. Managers therefore use tools such as quotas, closed seasons, minimum mesh sizes and protected breeding areas. Bycatch, the unintended catch of other species, is reduced by selective gear. Fishing communities have also been encouraged to take part in co-management, because fishers who help to make the rules are more likely to follow them.

In aquaculture, success depends on good seed and good water. Hatcheries produce fry from selected broodstock, and the fingerlings are stocked at a suitable density. Farmers must monitor water quality, especially dissolved oxygen, salinity and temperature, and they use aeration and probiotics to keep the pond healthy. Disease, such as white spot disease in shrimp, has caused heavy losses in the past. As a result, many farms have adopted better biosecurity, recirculating systems and more efficient feeds.

exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
A company in the Mekong Delta has produced pangasius for export for more than twenty years. In the early 2000s, it expanded quickly, and the ponds were stocked at high density. Several problems followed: fish became ill more often, antibiotics were used frequently and wastewater was discharged directly into the river. Some importers rejected shipments, and the company's reputation suffered.

Management decided to change. The company has built its own hatchery to produce healthy fingerlings, and it has reduced the stocking density by about 20 percent. Water quality is now measured twice a day with electronic probes, and aeration is switched on automatically when dissolved oxygen drops. Probiotics have replaced most antibiotics, and wastewater is treated in settling ponds before it leaves the farm. The company has also adopted a feed with a lower fishmeal content and a better feed conversion.

To prove these improvements, it applied for an aquaculture certification, which requires independent audits of environmental impact, animal health, food safety and working conditions. Every batch can be traced from the hatchery to the processing plant. Since certification, the company has regained several customers and obtained a price premium of about 8 percent. Survival rates have risen from 65 to 80 percent, and antibiotic use has fallen almost to zero. However, the manager admits that the changes have increased production costs, and that smaller neighbouring farms cannot afford the same investments. He therefore supports a cooperative approach, in which farmers share hatchery services, testing equipment and training.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · Agriculture and climate change
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Agriculture is both a victim and a cause of climate change. On the one hand, farmers, whose livelihoods depend on weather, are increasingly affected by drought, floods, heat stress and sea level rise. In river deltas, saltwater intrusion, which damages rice fields and fruit orchards, is becoming more serious. On the other hand, agriculture, forestry and other land use are responsible for roughly a quarter of global greenhouse gas emissions. Rice paddies and ruminant animals, which produce methane, and nitrogen fertilisers, which release nitrous oxide, are major sources, and land use change, such as the conversion of forest to farmland, adds further emissions.

Climate-smart agriculture aims to increase productivity, adapt to climate change and reduce emissions at the same time. Adaptation measures include drought-resistant and flood-tolerant varieties, changes in planting dates, diversified farming and improved irrigation. Mitigation measures include alternate wetting and drying, which reduces methane from paddies; efficient use of fertiliser; biogas systems that capture methane from manure; and agroforestry, which stores carbon in trees. Conservation agriculture, which combines minimum tillage, permanent soil cover and crop rotation, improves soil health and increases carbon sequestration.

Sustainability also means protecting ecosystems that support production. Excess nutrients that run off farmland can cause eutrophication, pollinators that visit crop flowers are threatened by pesticides, and soil degradation reduces future yields. Circular approaches, in which crop residues become feed, compost or biochar, reduce waste and costs. Governments, which set policy, and markets, which can reward good practice through certification and carbon credits, therefore play an important role alongside farmers.

exercises.title: Bài 2 · Case study: Saving water and carbon in rice farming
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
In a delta province where salt water enters the rivers during the dry season, rice farmers face two problems that threaten their livelihoods: water shortages and high production costs. A research institute, which works closely with the provincial extension service, proposed a package of practices that was tested on 200 farms.

The first practice was alternate wetting and drying (AWD), in which the fields are irrigated only when the water level falls 15 centimetres below the soil surface. Farmers who used a simple plastic tube to measure the level saved about 25 percent of irrigation water and reduced methane emissions by almost a third. The second practice was to reduce seed rates and nitrogen fertiliser, which cost less and lowered the risk of lodging and disease. The third was to collect rice straw, which used to be burnt in the field, and to use it for mushroom growing, compost and cattle feed. The farmers whose fields were selected also joined a group that shared a laser land-levelling machine.

The results over three seasons were encouraging. Yields remained stable, and costs fell by about 12 percent, so profits increased. The water saved allowed farmers to finish their crop before the saltwater arrived. The project, which was supported by a carbon-credit scheme, paid participants for the verified reduction in emissions. Nevertheless, some farmers were hesitant, because they were afraid that less water would reduce yields. Demonstration fields, which neighbours could visit, and the support of the cooperative helped to build trust. The case illustrates that practices which save money can also protect the climate, if farmers receive reliable advice.

content.why: Đoạn 2: đó là định nghĩa cách làm AWD trong dự án.

content.why: Đoạn 2: rơm được **thu gom** để trồng nấm, ủ phân và làm thức ăn gia súc.

exercises.title: Bài 1 · From farm to consumer: value chains
exercises.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.
exercises.instruction_vi: Đọc bài và trả lời câu hỏi (True = Đúng, False = Sai).
exercises.passage:
Most farmers do not sell directly to consumers. Instead, their products pass through a value chain: input suppliers provide seeds, fertiliser and feed; farmers produce the raw material; traders collect and transport it; processors clean, grade, pack or transform it; and retailers, including supermarkets and online platforms, deliver it to consumers. At each stage, costs are added and value may increase. However, farmers often receive only a small share of the final price, because they have little information and bargaining power, and because prices at the farmgate fluctuate with supply. As a result, price volatility is a major source of risk.

Several strategies can improve farmers' position. Joining a farmer group or cooperative allows them to sell larger volumes and to negotiate. Contract farming guarantees a buyer and sometimes provides inputs and technical advice, although farmers lose some flexibility. Value addition, such as drying, milling or making products from fruit, raises income, and branding or a geographical indication can protect a regional reputation. Access to credit and crop insurance helps farmers to invest and to survive bad years.

Export markets demand more. Buyers require compliance with quality standards, such as VietGAP or GlobalG.A.P., and a phytosanitary certificate is needed for plant products. Consequently, traceability and record keeping have become essential. Meanwhile, technology is changing agribusiness: sensors and drones support precision agriculture, farm management software tracks costs, and e-commerce connects producers directly with consumers. Nevertheless, technology will benefit smallholders only if it is affordable and accompanied by training.

A cooperative of 120 fruit growers in a delta province produced pomelos for many years, but the prices they received were low and unstable. Traders came to the farms, chose the best fruit and paid only a few thousand dong per kilogram. Although the fruit was of excellent flavour, it was sold unlabelled in local markets, and about 15 percent was lost after harvest because of poor handling.

The cooperative decided to move up the value chain. First, it registered a geographical indication for the pomelos of the area, which helped to protect the name and to distinguish the fruit from imitations. Second, the members adopted VietGAP and trained in safe pesticide use and record keeping; each fruit now has a QR code that links to the farm and the harvest date. Third, the cooperative built a small packing house with grading lines and a cold room, so that the fruit is sorted by size, wrapped and stored at the right temperature. A contract was signed with a supermarket chain, which pays a fixed premium for fruit that meets the standard, and a part of the harvest is sold through e-commerce platforms.

Within two years, the farmgate price had risen by about 40 percent, and post-harvest losses had fallen to 5 percent. Because the cooperative obtained a loan at a low interest rate, it was able to invest in drip irrigation, which improved fruit size. Drones are now used to monitor orchard health, and a free app tells members when to apply fertiliser. Despite these successes, challenges remain: the supermarket demands very large volumes, and a few members left because they preferred immediate cash from traders. The chairman nevertheless believes that cooperation, quality and branding are the only way for smallholders to capture more of the value of their products.
